# Mandelbulb Report Daniel Peterson

## History

    The Mandelbrot set is the definitive fractal. So it is no surprise that one
would contemplate its 3D anolog. This is exactly what Daniel White was determined to find
in late 2007; in his search for the "Holy Grail" of fractals. White was inspired by Rudy Rucker's early description
in "As Above, So Below", published 1987, as "a root - like object that's like a big sphere with a
dimple in the bottom and with bulbs on it, and further warts on the bulbs." So began White's earliest
attempts to render such a fractal along with his success. However, there was one major complication, and it
has to do with how the 2D version is defined. Mandelbrot's function operates on complex numbers and
so it is only defined in ℝ2. What is one to do in order to obtain this ellusive
bulb? We will explore this later.


> The world will freely offer itself to you to be unmasked, it has no choice, it will roll in ecstasy at your feet.

![8th order](https://users.soe.ucsc.edu/~pang/160/s15/projects/darpeter/report/order8.png)

* * *

![controls](https://users.soe.ucsc.edu/~pang/160/s15/projects/darpeter/report/controls.png)

## How to use

     This application has control panels for manipulating both the Mandelbulb formula and the rendering engine.
Together these controls can produce a variety of interesting scenes in real time.


Mandelbulb Controls

- **Order**: Changes the complexity by altering the power on the function.
- **Depth**: Changes the detail by altering iteration depth of the function.
- **Rotation**: Orients about the object's axes.

Render Controls

- **Fineness**: Changes the detail by altering the minimum distance to surface.
- **Zoom**: Changes the focal length of pinhole camera.
- **Eye**: Translates the camera in world space.

* * *

## How it works

### Mandelbulb Formula

     As mentioned briefly above there is no clear 3D analog for the 2D Mandelbrot set. This has purely
to do with the way complex numbers are defined. A complex has only two components and a specific algebra for multiplying
two of them together. One could define a third component, but then would have to invent some algebra for multiplying
these three component numbers. Let us call them "triplex."


     Multiplying triplex is important because the Mandelbrot function requires a triplex to be squared. One
could define this multiplication similar to the way it is defined for the two component complex, but the result is vaguely
Quarternion. One could even use a the Quarternion approach to extend the complex number into the 4th dimenstion, but these
renderings do not produce the warty structure Rucker first embossed in our minds.


     The solution to this problem is a bit of a hack. It is simple, clever and produces the features desired
for a 3D Mandelbrot set. It involves converting from a cartesian coordinate system into a polar one, and then performing
complex mulitplication using rotations. Let us see this method first applied on a two component complex number.


letc = (x, y)thenc' = (r, Θ)finally\|c2\| = \|c'2\| = (r2, 2Θ)

     This arithmetic is sound for multiplying complex numbers in polar form. However, what is
done next is not. The hack is now to perform this same method on a triplex by representing it in spherical form.
lett = (x, y, z)thent' = (r, Θ, Φ)and\|t2\| = \|t'2\| = (r2, 2Θ, 2Φ)finally\|tn\| = \|t'n\| = (rn, nΘ, nΦ)

     The Mandelbrot function now has leverage on the third dimension and one can perform the necessary triplex
multiplication. Notice how 'n' was used to generalize the power on the triplex. This is known as the "order" of the Mandelbulb.
After White had used this technique to render he was still scartching his head over the lack of complexity. It was not until a mathematician,
Paul Nylander, suggested "raising the power" on the function in order to increase the complexity of the fractal. It worked like
a charm and hence the generalized form. This is all summed up by the following formula known as "White and Nylander's nth
Power."
lets = some triplex in ℝ3andu = (r, Θ, Φ)thenZ(u)i = Z(u)ni-1 \+ v

![high order](https://users.soe.ucsc.edu/~pang/160/s15/projects/darpeter/report/repeat.png)

* * *

![top](https://users.soe.ucsc.edu/~pang/160/s15/projects/darpeter/report/top.png)

### Rendering

     The goal of this project was to produce an interactive Mandelbulb using ray casting;
which it does by using a handy performance tweak known as distance estimation. Conceptually, plain ray casting
is done by marching a ray some constant amount from an origin in the direction of a target surface. The surface is
then intersected by this ray and gives us a point in space. Ray casting is simple enough, but marching a constant
amount can be slow, so it must be sped up with distance estimation. Note that ray casting is also known as "sphere tracing",
becasue it is helpul to think of the amount marched as the radius of a sphere, this will become more apparent when distance
estimation is discussed.


     It is important to note that this application only ever defines two trianges; so x-y coordinates
are interpolated across the vertex-fragment interface. Meaning that all rendering is done on the GPU and this allows the application
to exploit its massively parallelized architecture. Specifically, rendering is done in the fragment shader and this is where the
raycast engine is specified. Describing exactly how to set up a raycaster is beyond the scope of this paper and so we will only discuss
the topic conceptually from now on. But in a nutshell, the fragment shader must define a ray from a camera and this unique x-y pair, then
compute an appropriate z value by marching this ray to an implicit surface defined by some formula, i.e. White and Nylander's nth
Power. See John C. Hart (1994) [Sphere Tracing: A Geometric Method for the Antialiased\\
Ray Tracing of Implicit Surfaces.](https://users.soe.ucsc.edu/~pang/160/s15/projects/darpeter/literature/rayCastingImplicitSurfaces.pdf)

     The real time nature of this application is due to distance estimation. Distance estimators are just
functions that return a safe distance for the ray to march without hitting the surface. So instead of moving in small
constant steps, it can move large distances along the ray with guarantee of not hitting the surface until some minimum
distance is reached; upon which the ray caster bails out. Back to the sphere analogy, one can visualize this procedure as a sequence of spheres with
decreasing radii to the surface. The smallest sphere is then the minimum distance specified for the raycaster to bail out on. This minimum distance
is important in terms of the Mandelbulb because it defines a level of detail in the fractal surface: smaller spheres are able to cut deeper into
the fractal and produce more complexity.


     John C. Hart did work with distance estimated 3D fractals back in 1989 [Ray Tracing Deterministic 3-D Fractals.](https://users.soe.ucsc.edu/~pang/160/s15/projects/darpeter/literature/distanceEstimating3DFractals.pdf) Specifically he used distance estimators to render 3D Julia sets using Quarternions. Using this paper
one could find a way to create a distance estimator for the Mandelbulb function defined above. Hint: use the chain rule.


letZ(u)i = Z(u)ni-1 \+ vthenZ'(u)i = nZ(u)n-1i-1 \\* Z'(u)ni-1 \+ 1finallyDE = 1/2 \* \|Z(u)\| / \|Z'(u)\| \* log(\|Z(u)\|)
     There are many ways to create distance estimators, but this method presented by Hart is good enough to approximate the surface.
It is important to realize that ray casting in general works by revelaing the surface through solving equations and not sampling data sets. The scene
is mathematically defined, and without this, real time would be impossible.

Algorithms and methods of plotting the Mandelbrot set on a computing device

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Fractal-zoom-1-03-Mandelbrot_Buzzsaw.png/250px-Fractal-zoom-1-03-Mandelbrot_Buzzsaw.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fractal-zoom-1-03-Mandelbrot_Buzzsaw.png) Still image [a movie of increasing magnification](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/07/Fractal-zoom-1-03-Mandelbrot_Buzzsaw.ogv) on 0.001643721971153 − 0.822467633298876 _i_[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Mandelbrot_sequence_new_still.png/250px-Mandelbrot_sequence_new_still.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mandelbrot_sequence_new_still.png) Still image of [an animation of increasing magnification](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/51/Mandelbrot_sequence_new.webm)

There are many programs and [algorithms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm "Algorithm") used to plot the [Mandelbrot set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set "Mandelbrot set") and other [fractals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractal "Fractal"), some of which are described in [fractal-generating software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractal-generating_software "Fractal-generating software"). These programs use a variety of algorithms to determine the color of individual [pixels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixel "Pixel") efficiently.

## Escape time algorithm

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Escape time algorithm")\]

The simplest algorithm for generating a representation of the Mandelbrot set is known as the "escape time" algorithm. A repeating calculation is performed for each _x_, _y_ point in the plot area and based on the behavior of that calculation, a color is chosen for that pixel.

### Unoptimized naïve escape time algorithm

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Unoptimized naïve escape time algorithm")\]

In both the unoptimized and optimized escape time algorithms, the _x_ and _y_ locations of each point are used as starting values in a repeating, or iterating calculation (described in detail below). The result of each iteration is used as the starting values for the next. The values are checked during each iteration to see whether they have reached a critical "escape" condition, or "bailout". If that condition is reached, the calculation is stopped, the pixel is drawn, and the next _x_, _y_ point is examined. For some starting values, escape occurs quickly, after only a small number of iterations. For starting values very close to but not in the set, it may take hundreds or thousands of iterations to escape. For values within the Mandelbrot set, escape will never occur. The programmer or user must choose how many iterations–or how much "depth"–they wish to examine. The higher the maximal number of iterations, the more detail and subtlety emerge in the final image, but the longer time it will take to calculate the fractal image.

Escape conditions can be simple or complex. Because no [complex number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number "Complex number") with a real or imaginary part greater than 2 can be part of the set, a common bailout is to escape when either coefficient exceeds 2. A more computationally complex method that detects escapes sooner, is to compute distance from the origin using the [Pythagorean theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagorean_theorem "Pythagorean theorem"), i.e., to determine the [absolute value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value "Absolute value"), or _modulus_, of the complex number. If this value exceeds 2, or equivalently, when the sum of the squares of the real and imaginary parts exceed 4, the point has reached escape. More computationally intensive rendering variations include the [Buddhabrot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhabrot "Buddhabrot") method, which finds escaping points and plots their iterated coordinates.

The color of each point represents how quickly the values reached the escape point. Often black is used to show values that fail to escape before the iteration limit, and gradually brighter colors are used for points that escape. This gives a visual representation of how many cycles were required before reaching the escape condition.

To render such an image, the region of the complex plane we are considering is subdivided into a certain number of [pixels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixel "Pixel"). To color any such pixel, let c{\\displaystyle c}![{\displaystyle c}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/86a67b81c2de995bd608d5b2df50cd8cd7d92455) be the midpoint of that pixel. We now iterate the critical point 0 under Pc{\\displaystyle P\_{c}}![{\displaystyle P_{c}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/7f5cb998e64c6e024e849f1aa1e5606209507710), checking at each step whether the orbit point has modulus larger than 2. When this is the case, we know that c{\\displaystyle c}![{\displaystyle c}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/86a67b81c2de995bd608d5b2df50cd8cd7d92455) does not belong to the Mandelbrot set, and we color our pixel according to the number of iterations used to find out. Otherwise, we keep iterating up to a fixed number of steps, after which we decide that our parameter is "probably" in the Mandelbrot set, or at least very close to it, and color the pixel black.

In [pseudocode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudocode "Pseudocode"), this algorithm would look as follows. The algorithm does not use complex numbers and manually simulates complex-number operations using two real numbers, for those who do not have a [complex data type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_data_type "Complex data type"). The program may be simplified if the programming language includes complex-data-type operations.

```
for each pixel (Px, Py) on the screen do
    x0 := scaled x coordinate of pixel (scaled to lie in the Mandelbrot X scale (-2.00, 0.47))
    y0 := scaled y coordinate of pixel (scaled to lie in the Mandelbrot Y scale (-1.12, 1.12))
    x := 0.0
    y := 0.0
    iteration := 0
    max_iteration := 1000
    while (x*x + y*y ≤ 2*2 AND iteration < max_iteration) do
        xtemp := x*x - y*y + x0
        y := 2*x*y + y0
        x := xtemp
        iteration := iteration + 1

    color := palette[iteration]
    plot(Px, Py, color)
```

Here, relating the pseudocode to c{\\displaystyle c}![{\displaystyle c}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/86a67b81c2de995bd608d5b2df50cd8cd7d92455), z{\\displaystyle z}![{\displaystyle z}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/bf368e72c009decd9b6686ee84a375632e11de98) and Pc{\\displaystyle P\_{c}}![{\displaystyle P_{c}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/7f5cb998e64c6e024e849f1aa1e5606209507710):

- z=x+iy{\\displaystyle z=x+iy\ }![{\displaystyle z=x+iy\ }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/28f5a0cda384cffc6dfe2b5d2590d0407501b125)
- z2=x2+2ixy{\\displaystyle z^{2}=x^{2}+2ixy}![{\displaystyle z^{2}=x^{2}+2ixy}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/9509d827c802ee1530fac95092d9b6873dc1894c) \- y2{\\displaystyle y^{2}\ }![{\displaystyle y^{2}\ }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/e8fe373d91df5c0daf77f83af51cd2a872cea0c6)
- c=x0+iy0{\\displaystyle c=x\_{0}+iy\_{0}\ }![{\displaystyle c=x_{0}+iy_{0}\ }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/9556f96bb6e42fdb14d58bd8ce3854257aafca62)

and so, as can be seen in the pseudocode in the computation of _x_ and _y_:

- x=Re⁡(z2+c)=x2−y2+x0{\\displaystyle x=\\mathop {\\mathrm {Re} } (z^{2}+c)=x^{2}-y^{2}+x\_{0}}![{\displaystyle x=\mathop {\mathrm {Re} } (z^{2}+c)=x^{2}-y^{2}+x_{0}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/b18a3233ed63d7bff11463a0e6683b9a085a14a0) and y=Im⁡(z2+c)=2xy+y0.{\\displaystyle y=\\mathop {\\mathrm {Im} } (z^{2}+c)=2xy+y\_{0}.\ }![{\displaystyle y=\mathop {\mathrm {Im} } (z^{2}+c)=2xy+y_{0}.\ }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/94923ff5c86dcb580db28b4146ae1cdcfb93e9c6)

To get colorful images of the set, the assignment of a color to each value of the number of executed iterations can be made using one of a variety of functions (linear, exponential, etc.). One practical way, without slowing down calculations, is to use the number of executed iterations as an entry to a [palette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palette_(computing) "Palette (computing)") initialized at startup. If the color table has, for instance, 500 entries, then the color selection is _n_ mod500, where _n_ is the number of iterations.

### Optimized escape time algorithms

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Optimized escape time algorithms")\]

The code in the previous section uses an unoptimized inner while loop for clarity. In the unoptimized version, one must perform five multiplications per iteration. To reduce the number of multiplications the following code for the inner while loop may be used instead:

```
x2:= 0
y2:= 0
w:= 0

while (x2 + y2 ≤ 4 and iteration < max_iteration) do
    x:= x2 - y2 + x0
    y:= w - x2 - y2 + y0
    x2:= x * x
    y2:= y * y
    w:= (x + y) * (x + y)
    iteration:= iteration + 1
```

The above code works via some algebraic simplification of the complex multiplication:

(iy+x)2=−y2+2iyx+x2=x2−y2+2iyx{\\displaystyle {\\begin{aligned}(iy+x)^{2}&=-y^{2}+2iyx+x^{2}\\\&=x^{2}-y^{2}+2iyx\\end{aligned}}}![{\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}(iy+x)^{2}&=-y^{2}+2iyx+x^{2}\\&=x^{2}-y^{2}+2iyx\end{aligned}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/53680df327ea84785301588b8990d1026c61fbd0)

Using the above identity, the number of multiplications can be reduced to three instead of five.

The above inner while loop can be further optimized by expanding _w_ to

w=x2+2xy+y2{\\displaystyle w=x^{2}+2xy+y^{2}}![{\displaystyle w=x^{2}+2xy+y^{2}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/aa4d8e0c7be50dbc4c99cf4f831f8806d2e0ddba)

Substituting _w_ into y=w−x2−y2+y0{\\displaystyle y=w-x^{2}-y^{2}+y\_{0}}![{\displaystyle y=w-x^{2}-y^{2}+y_{0}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/10bf0df3c49ab3567d85a7a95f66a26d81ce855e) yields
y=2xy+y0{\\displaystyle y=2xy+y\_{0}}![{\displaystyle y=2xy+y_{0}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/031c0fc9071b9c4619ecd14c1921eba6e133f98d)
and hence calculating _w_ is no longer needed.

The further optimized pseudocode for the above is:

```
x:= 0
y:= 0
x2:= 0
y2:= 0

while (x2 + y2 ≤ 4 and iteration < max_iteration) do
    x2:= x * x
    y2:= y * y
    y:= 2 * x * y + y0
    x:= x2 - y2 + x0
    iteration:= iteration + 1
```

Note that in the above pseudocode, 2xy{\\displaystyle 2xy}![{\displaystyle 2xy}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0cf28a82088fc2021c794fee1de241f90622d5ae) seems to increase the number of multiplications by 1, but since 2 is the multiplier the code can be optimized via (x+x)y{\\displaystyle (x+x)y}![{\displaystyle (x+x)y}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/a8d21a98ce454db1b3a5ac18e7d23dcf17e0d129).

## Coloring algorithms

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Coloring algorithms")\]

In addition to plotting the set, a variety of algorithms have been developed to

- efficiently color the set in an aesthetically pleasing way
- show structures of the data (scientific visualisation)

### Histogram coloring

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Histogram coloring")\]

|     |     |
| --- | --- |
| [![icon](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg) | This section **needs [more citations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Please help [improve this article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set "Special:EditPage/Plotting algorithms for the Mandelbrot set") by [adding citations to reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners "Help:Referencing for beginners") in this section. Unsourced material may be challenged and removed._(June 2019)__([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ |

A more complex coloring method involves using a [histogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histogram "Histogram") which pairs each pixel with said pixel's maximum iteration count before escape/bailout. This method will equally distribute colors to the same overall area, and, importantly, is independent of the maximum number of iterations chosen.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set#cite_note-1)

This algorithm has four passes. The first pass involves calculating the iteration counts associated with each pixel (but without any pixels being plotted). These are stored in an array `IterationCounts[x][y]`, where `x` and `y` are the x and y coordinates of said pixel on the screen respectively.

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Mandelbrot-no-histogram-coloring-10000-iterations.png/250px-Mandelbrot-no-histogram-coloring-10000-iterations.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mandelbrot-no-histogram-coloring-10000-iterations.png) | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Mandelbrot-no-histogram-coloring-1000-iterations.png/250px-Mandelbrot-no-histogram-coloring-1000-iterations.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mandelbrot-no-histogram-coloring-1000-iterations.png) | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Mandelbrot-no-histogram-coloring-100-iterations.png/250px-Mandelbrot-no-histogram-coloring-100-iterations.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mandelbrot-no-histogram-coloring-100-iterations.png) |
| [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Mandelbrot-histogram-10000-iterations.png/250px-Mandelbrot-histogram-10000-iterations.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mandelbrot-histogram-10000-iterations.png) | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Mandelbrot-histogram-1000-iterations.png/250px-Mandelbrot-histogram-1000-iterations.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mandelbrot-histogram-1000-iterations.png) | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Mandelbrot-histogram-100-iterations.png/250px-Mandelbrot-histogram-100-iterations.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mandelbrot-histogram-100-iterations.png) |
| The top row is a series of plots using the escape time algorithm for 10000, 1000 and 100 maximum iterations per pixel respectively. The bottom row uses the same maximum iteration values but utilizes the histogram coloring method. Notice how little the coloring changes per different maximum iteration counts for the histogram coloring method plots. |

The first step of the second pass is to create an array `NumIterationsPerPixel[n]`, where the array size `n` is the maximum iteration count. Next, one must iterate over the array of pixel-iteration count pairs `IterationCounts[x][y]`, and retrieve each pixel's saved iteration count, _i_, via e.g. `i = IterationCounts[x][y]`. After each pixel's iteration count _i_ is retrieved, it is necessary to index the `NumIterationsPerPixel` array at _i_ and increment the indexed value (which is initially zero) -- e.g. `NumIterationsPerPixel[i] = NumIterationsPerPixel[i] + 1`.

```
for (x = 0; x < width; x++) do
    for (y = 0; y < height; y++) do
        i:= IterationCounts[x][y]
        NumIterationsPerPixel[i]++
```

The third pass iterates through the NumIterationsPerPixel array and adds up all the stored values, saving them in _total_. The array index represents the number of pixels that reached that iteration count before bailout.

```
total: = 0
for (i = 0; i < max_iterations; i++) do
    total += NumIterationsPerPixel[i]
```

After this, the fourth pass begins and all the values in the IterationCounts array are indexed, and, for each iteration count _i_, associated with each pixel, the count is added to a global sum of all the iteration counts from 1 to _i_ in the NumIterationsPerPixel array . This value is then normalized by dividing the sum by the _total_ value computed earlier.

```
hue[][]:= 0.0
for (x = 0; x < width; x++) do
    for (y = 0; y < height; y++) do
        iteration:= IterationCounts[x][y]
        for (i = 0; i <= iteration; i++) do
            hue[x][y] += NumIterationsPerPixel[i] / total /* Must be floating-point division. */

...

color = palette[hue[m, n]]

...
```

Finally, the computed value is used, e.g. as an index to a color palette.

This method may be combined with the smooth coloring method below for more aesthetically pleasing images.

### Continuous (smooth) coloring

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Continuous (smooth) coloring")\]

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Escape_Time_Algorithm_bands.png/250px-Escape_Time_Algorithm_bands.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Escape_Time_Algorithm_bands.png)

This image was rendered with the escape time algorithm. There are very obvious "bands" of color

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Normalized_Iteration_Count_Algorithm_1.png/250px-Normalized_Iteration_Count_Algorithm_1.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Normalized_Iteration_Count_Algorithm_1.png)

This image was rendered with the normalized iteration count algorithm. The bands of color have been replaced by a smooth gradient. Also, the colors take on the same pattern that would be observed if the escape time algorithm were used.

The escape time algorithm is popular for its simplicity. However, it creates bands of color, which, as a type of [aliasing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aliasing "Aliasing"), can detract from an image's aesthetic value. This can be improved using an algorithm known as "normalized iteration count",[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set#cite_note-3) which provides a smooth transition of colors between iterations. The algorithm associates a real number ν{\\displaystyle \\nu }![{\displaystyle \nu }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c15bbbb971240cf328aba572178f091684585468) with each value of _z_ by using the connection of the iteration number with the [potential function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_set#The_potential_function_and_the_real_iteration_number "Julia set"). This function is given by

ϕ(z)=limn→∞(log⁡\|zn\|/Pn),{\\displaystyle \\phi (z)=\\lim \_{n\\to \\infty }(\\log \|z\_{n}\|/P^{n}),}![{\displaystyle \phi (z)=\lim _{n\to \infty }(\log |z_{n}|/P^{n}),}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/65464fe69c4bb8f0fe064677d1e2ecea419f4349)

where _z_ _n_ is the value after _n_ iterations and _P_ is the power for which _z_ is raised to in the Mandelbrot set equation ( _z_ _n_ +1= _z_ _n__P_+ _c_, _P_ is generally 2).

If we choose a large bailout radius _N_ (e.g., 10100), we have that

log⁡\|zn\|/Pn=log⁡(N)/Pν(z){\\displaystyle \\log \|z\_{n}\|/P^{n}=\\log(N)/P^{\\nu (z)}}![{\displaystyle \log |z_{n}|/P^{n}=\log(N)/P^{\nu (z)}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/00425db01548d98a2b68b40796494d4b18d98b2c)

for some real number ν(z){\\displaystyle \\nu (z)}![{\displaystyle \nu (z)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c81dc7d5776cf7cff79847492782c3db6e69421c), and this is

ν(z)=n−logP⁡(log⁡\|zn\|/log⁡(N)),{\\displaystyle \\nu (z)=n-\\log \_{P}(\\log \|z\_{n}\|/\\log(N)),}![{\displaystyle \nu (z)=n-\log _{P}(\log |z_{n}|/\log(N)),}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/42663447fb5a0b29ca1c7a973fe67879fe062cc0)

and as _n_ is the first iteration number such that \| _z_ _n_\| \> _N_, the number we subtract from _n_ is in the interval \[0,1).\
\
For the coloring we must have a cyclic scale of colors (constructed mathematically, for instance) and containing _H_ colors numbered from 0 to _H_ −1 ( _H_ =500, for instance). We multiply the real number ν(z){\\displaystyle \\nu (z)}![{\displaystyle \nu (z)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c81dc7d5776cf7cff79847492782c3db6e69421c) by a fixed real number determining the density of the colors in the picture, take the integral part of this number modulo _H_, and use it to look up the corresponding color in the color table.\
\
For example, modifying the above pseudocode and also using the concept of [linear interpolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_interpolation "Linear interpolation") would yield\
\
```\
for each pixel (Px, Py) on the screen do\
    x0:= scaled x coordinate of pixel (scaled to lie in the Mandelbrot X scale (-2.5, 1))\
    y0:= scaled y coordinate of pixel (scaled to lie in the Mandelbrot Y scale (-1, 1))\
    x:= 0.0\
    y:= 0.0\
    iteration:= 0\
    max_iteration:= 1000\
    // Here N = 2^8 is chosen as a reasonable bailout radius.\
\
    while x*x + y*y ≤ (1 << 16) and iteration < max_iteration do\
        xtemp:= x*x - y*y + x0\
        y:= 2*x*y + y0\
        x:= xtemp\
        iteration:= iteration + 1\
\
    // Used to avoid floating point issues with points inside the set.\
    if iteration < max_iteration then\
        // sqrt of inner term removed using log simplification rules.\
        log_zn:= log(x*x + y*y) / 2\
        nu:= log(log_zn / log(2)) / log(2)\
        // Rearranging the potential function.\
        // Dividing log_zn by log(2) instead of log(N = 1<<8)\
        // because we want the entire palette to range from the\
        // center to radius 2, NOT our bailout radius.\
        iteration:= iteration + 1 - nu\
\
    color1:= palette[floor(iteration)]\
    color2:= palette[floor(iteration) + 1]\
    // iteration % 1 = fractional part of iteration.\
    color:= linear_interpolate(color1, color2, iteration % 1)\
    plot(Px, Py, color)\
```\
\
### Exponentially mapped and cyclic iterations\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Exponentially mapped and cyclic iterations")\]\
\
[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/CyclicColoringLch.png/250px-CyclicColoringLch.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CyclicColoringLch.png) Exponential Cyclic Coloring in LCH color space with shading\
\
Typically when we render a fractal, the range of where colors from a given palette appear along the fractal is static. If we desire to offset the location from the border of the fractal, or adjust their palette to cycle in a specific way, there are a few simple changes we can make when taking the final iteration count before passing it along to choose an item from our palette.\
\
When we have obtained the iteration count, we can make the range of colors non-linear. Raising a value normalized to the range \[0,1\] to a power _n_, maps a linear range to an exponential range, which in our case can nudge the appearance of colors along the outside of the fractal, and allow us to bring out other colors, or push in the entire palette closer to the border.\
\
v=((i/maxi)SN)1.5modN{\\displaystyle v=((\\mathbf {i} /max\_{i})^{\\mathbf {S} }\\mathbf {N} )^{1.5}{\\bmod {\\mathbf {N} }}}![{\displaystyle v=((\mathbf {i} /max_{i})^{\mathbf {S} }\mathbf {N} )^{1.5}{\bmod {\mathbf {N} }}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/7ff792a91632008038aded85f13886a3e30827e3)\
\
where **i** is our iteration count after bailout, **max\_i** is our iteration limit, **S** is the exponent we are raising iters to, and **N** is the number of items in our palette. This scales the iter count non-linearly and scales the palette to cycle approximately proportionally to the zoom.\
\
We can then plug v into whatever algorithm we desire for generating a color.\
\
### Passing iterations into a color directly\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Passing iterations into a color directly")\]\
\
[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/LCH_COLORING.png/330px-LCH_COLORING.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LCH_COLORING.png) Example of exponentially mapped cyclic LCH coloring without shading\
\
One thing we may want to consider is avoiding having to deal with a palette or color blending at all. There are actually a handful of methods we can leverage to generate smooth, consistent coloring by constructing the color on the spot.\
\
#### v refers to a normalized exponentially mapped cyclic iter count\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: v refers to a normalized exponentially mapped cyclic iter count")\]\
\
#### f(v) refers to the [sRGB transfer function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SRGB\#Transfer_function_(%22gamma%22) "SRGB")\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: f(v) refers to the sRGB transfer function")\]\
\
A naive method for generating a color in this way is by directly scaling **v** to 255 and passing it into RGB as such\
\
```\
rgb = [v * 255, v * 255, v * 255]\
```\
\
One flaw with this is that RGB is non-linear due to gamma; consider linear sRGB instead. Going from RGB to sRGB uses an inverse companding function on the channels. This makes the gamma linear, and allows us to properly sum the colors for sampling.\
\
```\
srgb = [v * 255, v * 255, v * 255]\
```\
\
[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/HSV_Gradient_Example.png/330px-HSV_Gradient_Example.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HSV_Gradient_Example.png) HSV Gradient\
\
### HSV coloring\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: HSV coloring")\]\
\
HSV Coloring can be accomplished by mapping iter count from \[0,max\_iter) to \[0,360), taking it to the power of 1.5, and then modulo 360.\
h=((i/maxi)360)1.5mod360{\\displaystyle h=((i/max\_{i})360)^{1.5}{\\bmod {3}}60}![{\displaystyle h=((i/max_{i})360)^{1.5}{\bmod {3}}60}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/b8b4eccf3b1575a2397858eedeb2981cd3022e24)\
We can then simply take the exponentially mapped iter count into the value and return\
\
```\
hsv = [powf((i / max) * 360, 1.5) % 360, 100, (i / max) * 100]\
```\
\
This method applies to HSL as well, except we pass a saturation of 50% instead.\
\
```\
hsl = [powf((i / max) * 360, 1.5) % 360, 50, (i / max) * 100]\
```\
\

\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: LCH coloring")\]\
\
One of the most perceptually uniform coloring methods involves passing in the processed iter count into LCH. If we utilize the exponentially mapped and cyclic method above, we can take the result of that into the Luma and Chroma channels. We can also exponentially map the iter count and scale it to 360, and pass this modulo 360 into the hue.\
\

One issue we wish to avoid here is out-of-gamut colors. This can be achieved with a little trick based on the change in in-gamut colors relative to luma and chroma. As we increase luma, we need to decrease chroma to stay within gamut.\
\
```\

v = 1.0 - powf(cos(pi * s), 2.0);\

\

In addition to the simple and slow escape time algorithms already discussed, there are many other more advanced algorithms that can be used to speed up the plotting process.\

### Distance estimates\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Distance estimates")\]\
\
One can compute the [distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance "Distance") from point _c_ (in [exterior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exterior_(topology) "Exterior (topology)") or [interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior_(topology) "Interior (topology)")) to nearest point on the [boundary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boundary_(topology) "Boundary (topology)") of the Mandelbrot set.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set#cite_note-Albert_Lobo-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set#cite_note-5)\
\
#### Exterior distance estimation\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Exterior distance estimation")\]\
\
The proof of the [connectedness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandelbrot_set#Basic_properties "Mandelbrot set") of the Mandelbrot set in fact gives a formula for the [uniformizing map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_ray#Uniformization "External ray") of the [complement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complement_(set_theory) "Complement (set theory)") of M{\\displaystyle M}![{\displaystyle M}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f82cade9898ced02fdd08712e5f0c0151758a0dd) (and the [derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative "Derivative") of this map). By the [Koebe quarter theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koebe_quarter_theorem "Koebe quarter theorem"), one can then estimate the distance between the midpoint of our [pixel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixel "Pixel") and the Mandelbrot set up to a factor of 4.\
\
In other words, provided that the maximal number of iterations is sufficiently high, one obtains a picture of the Mandelbrot set with the following properties:\
\
1. Every pixel that contains a point of the Mandelbrot set is colored black.\
2. Every pixel that is colored black is close to the Mandelbrot set.\
\
[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Demm_2000_Mandelbrot_set.jpg/250px-Demm_2000_Mandelbrot_set.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Demm_2000_Mandelbrot_set.jpg) Exterior distance estimate may be used to color whole complement of Mandelbrot set\
\

\

\
From a mathematician's point of view, this formula only works in limit where _n_ goes to infinity, but very reasonable estimates can be found with just a few additional iterations after the main loop exits.\
\
Once _b_ is found, by the Koebe 1/4-theorem, we know that there is no point of the Mandelbrot set with distance from _c_ smaller than _b/4_.\

#### Interior distance estimation\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Interior distance estimation")\]\
\
[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Mandelbrot_Interior_600.png/250px-Mandelbrot_Interior_600.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mandelbrot_Interior_600.png) Pixels colored according to the estimated interior distance\

### Periodicity checking\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Periodicity checking")\]\
\
To prevent having to do huge numbers of iterations for points inside the set, one can perform periodicity checking, which checks whether a point reached in iterating a pixel has been reached before. If so, the pixel cannot diverge and must be in the set. Periodicity checking is a trade-off, as the need to remember points costs data management instructions and memory, but saves computational instructions. However, checking against only one previous iteration can detect many periods with little performance overhead. For example, within the while loop of the pseudocode above, make the following modifications:\
\
```\
xold := 0\
yold := 0\
period := 0\
while (x*x + y*y ≤ 2*2 and iteration < max_iteration) do\
    xtemp := x*x - y*y + x0\
    y := 2*x*y + y0\
    x := xtemp\
    iteration := iteration + 1\
\
    if x ≈ xold and y ≈ yold then\
        iteration := max_iteration  /* Set to max for the color plotting */\
        break        /* We are inside the Mandelbrot set, leave the while loop */\
\
    period:= period + 1\
    if period > 20 then\
        period := 0\
        xold := x\
        yold := y\
```\
\
The above code stores away a new x and y value on every 20th iteration, thus it can detect periods that are up to 20 points long.\
\
### Border tracing / edge checking\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Border tracing / edge checking")\]\
\
[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Mandelbrot_DEM_Sobel.png/250px-Mandelbrot_DEM_Sobel.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mandelbrot_DEM_Sobel.png) Edge detection using [Sobel filter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobel_filter "Sobel filter") of hyperbolic components of Mandelbrot set\
\
Because the Mandelbrot set is [full](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_set_(topology) "Full set (topology)"),[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set#cite_note-Proof_of_connectedness-12) any point enclosed by a closed shape whose borders lie entirely within the Mandelbrot set must itself be in the Mandelbrot set. Border tracing works by following the [lemniscates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_lemniscate "Polynomial lemniscate") of the various iteration levels (colored bands) all around the set, and then filling the entire band at once. This also provides a speed increase because large numbers of points can be now skipped.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set#cite_note-13)\
\
[Play video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Boundary_following_movie.webm "Play video") Duration: 7 seconds.0:07Animation of border tracing\
\
In the animation shown, points outside the set are colored with a 1000-iteration escape time algorithm. Tracing the set border and filling it, rather than iterating the interior points, reduces the total number of iterations by 93.16%. With a higher iteration limit the benefit would be even greater.\
\
### Rectangle checking\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Rectangle checking")\]\
\
Rectangle checking is an older and simpler method for plotting the Mandelbrot set. The basic idea of rectangle checking is that if every pixel in a rectangle's border shares the same amount of iterations, then the rectangle can be safely filled using that number of iterations. There are several variations of the rectangle checking method, however, all of them are slower than the border tracing method because they end up calculating more pixels. One variant just calculates the corner pixels of each rectangle, however, this causes damaged pictures more often than calculating the entire border, thus it only works reasonably well if only small boxes of around 6x6 pixels are used, and no recursing in from bigger boxes. ( [Fractint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractint "Fractint") method.)\
\
The most simple rectangle checking method lies in checking the borders of equally sized rectangles, resembling a grid pattern. (Mariani's algorithm.)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set#cite_note-14)\
\
A faster and slightly more advanced variant is to first calculate a bigger box, say 25x25 pixels. If the entire box border has the same color, then just fill the box with the same color. If not, then split the box into four boxes of 13x13 pixels, reusing the already calculated pixels as outer border, and sharing the inner "cross" pixels between the inner boxes. Again, fill in those boxes that has only one border color. And split those boxes that don't, now into four 7x7 pixel boxes. And then those that "fail" into 4x4 boxes. (Mariani-Silver algorithm.)\
\
Even faster is to split the boxes in half instead of into four boxes. Then it might be optimal to use boxes with a 1.4:1 [aspect ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspect_ratio "Aspect ratio"), so they can be split like [how A3 papers are folded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_216 "ISO 216") into A4 and A5 papers. (The DIN approach.)\
\
As with border tracing, rectangle checking only works on areas with one discrete color. But even if the outer area uses smooth/continuous coloring then rectangle checking will still speed up the costly inner area of the Mandelbrot set. Unless the inner area also uses some smooth coloring method, for instance [interior distance estimation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set#Interior_distance_estimation).\
\
### Symmetry utilization\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Symmetry utilization")\]\
\
The horizontal symmetry of the Mandelbrot set allows for portions of the rendering process to be skipped upon the presence of the real axis in the final image. However, regardless of the portion that gets mirrored, the same number of points will be rendered.\
\
Julia sets have symmetry around the origin. This means that quadrant 1 and quadrant 3 are symmetric, and quadrants 2 and quadrant 4 are symmetric. Supporting symmetry for both Mandelbrot and Julia sets requires handling symmetry differently for the two different types of graphs.\
\
### Multithreading\
\
\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Multithreading")\]\
\
Escape-time rendering of Mandelbrot and Julia sets lends itself extremely well to parallel processing. On multi-core machines the area to be plotted can be divided into a series of rectangular areas which can then be provided as a set of tasks to be rendered by a pool of rendering threads. This is an [embarrassingly parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embarrassingly_parallel "Embarrassingly parallel")[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set#cite_note-15) computing problem. (Note that one gets the best speed-up by first excluding symmetric areas of the plot, and then dividing the remaining unique regions into rectangular areas.)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotting_algorithms_for_the_Mandelbrot_set#cite_note-16)\

\
Now from the original definition:\
\

\
It follows that:\
\

\
As the iterative relationship relates an arbitrary point to the central point by a very small change δ{\\displaystyle \\delta }![{\displaystyle \delta }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c5321cfa797202b3e1f8620663ff43c4660ea03a), then most of the iterations of ϵn{\\displaystyle \\epsilon \_{n}}![{\displaystyle \epsilon _{n}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/32b4644a36a17b4d9be4d81de5293064a5413d15) are also small and can be calculated using floating point hardware.\
\
However, for every arbitrary point in the disc it is possible to calculate a value for a given ϵn{\\displaystyle \\epsilon \_{n}}![{\displaystyle \epsilon _{n}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/32b4644a36a17b4d9be4d81de5293064a5413d15) without having to iterate through the sequence from ϵ0{\\displaystyle \\epsilon \_{0}}![{\displaystyle \epsilon _{0}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d2cae6289b0fe626d1f9472a3416ac73e87bc5a3), by expressing ϵn{\\displaystyle \\epsilon \_{n}}![{\displaystyle \epsilon _{n}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/32b4644a36a17b4d9be4d81de5293064a5413d15) as a [power series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_series "Power series") of δ{\\displaystyle \\delta }![{\displaystyle \delta }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c5321cfa797202b3e1f8620663ff43c4660ea03a).\
\

\

\

\

\

The coefficients in the power series can be calculated as iterative series using only values from the central point's iterations z{\\displaystyle z}![{\displaystyle z}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/bf368e72c009decd9b6686ee84a375632e11de98), and do not change for any arbitrary point in the disc. If δ{\\displaystyle \\delta }![{\displaystyle \delta }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c5321cfa797202b3e1f8620663ff43c4660ea03a) is very small, ϵn{\\displaystyle \\epsilon \_{n}}![{\displaystyle \epsilon _{n}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/32b4644a36a17b4d9be4d81de5293064a5413d15) should be calculable to sufficient accuracy using only a few terms of the power series. As the Mandelbrot Escape Contours are 'continuous' over the complex plane, if a point's escape time has been calculated, then the escape time of that point's neighbours should be similar. Interpolation of the neighbouring points should provide a good estimation of where to start in the ϵn{\\displaystyle \\epsilon \_{n}}![{\displaystyle \epsilon _{n}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/32b4644a36a17b4d9be4d81de5293064a5413d15) series.\
\
Further, separate interpolation of both real axis points and imaginary axis points should provide both an upper and lower bound for the point being calculated. If both results are the same (i.e. both escape or do not escape) then the difference Δn{\\displaystyle \\Delta n}![{\displaystyle \Delta n}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/31f0672c38daf81ebe64b7828c72883b52d2d261) can be used to recuse until both an upper and lower bound can be established. If floating point hardware can be used to iterate the ϵ{\\displaystyle \\epsilon }![{\displaystyle \epsilon }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c3837cad72483d97bcdde49c85d3b7b859fb3fd2) series, then there exists a relation between how many iterations can be achieved in the time it takes to use BigNum software to compute a given ϵn{\\displaystyle \\epsilon \_{n}}![{\displaystyle \epsilon _{n}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/32b4644a36a17b4d9be4d81de5293064a5413d15). If the difference between the bounds is greater than the number of iterations, it is possible to perform binary search using BigNum software, successively halving the gap until it becomes more time efficient to find the escape value using floating point hardware.\

// This is my power function, based on the standard spherical coordinates as defined here:

// http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical\_coordinate\_system

//

// It seems to be similar to the one Quilez uses:

// http://www.iquilezles.org/www/articles/mandelbulb/mandelbulb.htm

//

// Notice the north and south poles are different here.

void powN1(inoutvec3 z, float r, inoutfloat dr) {

// extract polar coordinates

float theta =acos(z.z/r);

float phi =atan(z.y,z.x);

dr =pow( r, Power-1.0)\*Power\*dr +1.0;

// scale and rotate the point

float zr =pow( r,Power);

theta = theta\*Power;

phi = phi\*Power;

// convert back to cartesian coordinates

z = zr\*vec3(sin(theta)\*cos(phi), sin(phi)\*sin(theta), cos(theta));

}

// This is a power function taken from the implementation by Enforcer:

// http://www.fractalforums.com/mandelbulb-implementation/realtime-renderingoptimisations/

//

// I cannot follow its derivation from spherical coordinates,

// but it does give a nice mandelbrot like object for Power=2

void powN2(inoutvec3 z, float zr0, inoutfloat dr) {

float zo0 =asin( z.z/zr0 );

float zi0 =atan( z.y,z.x );

float zr =pow( zr0, Power-1.0 );

float zo = zo0 \* Power;

float zi = zi0 \* Power;

dr = zr\*dr\*Power +1.0;

zr \*= zr0;

z = zr\*vec3( cos(zo)\*cos(zi), cos(zo)\*sin(zi), sin(zo) );

}

# Mandelbulb

AraEveLeoSal

1x

The **Mandelbulb** is a three-dimensional [fractal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal) object that extends the iconic two-dimensional [Mandelbrot set](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbrot_set) into three dimensions, characterized by infinite [self-similarity](https://grokipedia.com/page/Self-similarity) and intricate, bulbous structures resembling natural forms like [Romanesco broccoli](https://grokipedia.com/page/Romanesco_broccoli).[\[1\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-1)[\[2\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-2) Developed collaboratively by amateur [fractal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal) enthusiasts Daniel White and Paul Nylander, it emerged from experiments beginning in November 2007 on the [Fractal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal) Forums [online community](https://grokipedia.com/page/Online_community), with White publishing the initial formula and Nylander refining it by incorporating higher powers for enhanced detail.[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3)[\[1\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-1)Mathematically, the Mandelbulb is defined in spherical coordinates (ρ,θ,ϕ)(\\rho, \\theta, \\phi)(ρ,θ,ϕ) by iterating the map Tc(X)=Xn+cT\_c(X) = X^n + cTc​(X)=Xn+c, where Xn=(ρn,nθ,nϕ)X^n = (\\rho^n, n\\theta, n\\phi)Xn=(ρn,nθ,nϕ) and nnn is typically 8 to achieve balanced fractal complexity, with the set comprising points ccc for which the orbit of the origin remains bounded.[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3)[\[4\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-4) This geometric iteration avoids traditional complex numbers, instead using polar decomposition to scale the radius and multiply the angles, producing a structure with exquisite detail across all axes when rendered at high resolutions.[\[4\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-4)[\[2\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-2)First rendered in three dimensions by Thomas Ludwig in 2007 and gaining widespread attention in 2009 through deep zooms revealing endless budding patterns, the Mandelbulb has inspired software tools like Mandelbulb3D for exploration and artistic visualization.[\[2\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-2)[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3) Unlike the [Mandelbrot set](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbrot_set), whose connectivity is mathematically proven, the Mandelbulb's topological properties—such as whether its body is simply connected—remain an open research question in [fractal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal) geometry.[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3) Its discovery highlighted the potential for community-driven innovation in [mathematics](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mathematics), blending [computation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Computation), [art](https://grokipedia.com/page/Art), and natural [pattern recognition](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pattern_recognition).[\[1\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-1)[\[5\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-5)

## Introduction

### Definition

The Mandelbulb is a three-dimensional [fractal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal) defined as the set of points $ c = (x\_c, y\_c, z\_c) \\in \\mathbb{R}^3 $ such that the sequence of iterates $ v\_0 = 0 $, $ v\_{k+1} = v\_k^n + c $ remains bounded for all $ k $, where $ n \\geq 2 $ is typically an even [integer](https://grokipedia.com/page/Integer) and the power operation is interpreted in spherical coordinates to extend the geometry of the two-dimensional [Mandelbrot set](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbrot_set).[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3) This boundedness condition mirrors the [Mandelbrot set](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbrot_set)'s definition in the [complex plane](https://grokipedia.com/page/Complex_plane), where points $ c $ yield orbits under squaring and translation that do not escape to infinity.[\[4\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-4)To apply the power $ n $, a vector $ v = (x, y, z) $ is first transformed into spherical coordinates: $ r = \\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} $, $ \\theta = \\arccos(z / r) $ (the polar angle from the positive z-axis), and $ \\phi = \\atan2(y, x) $ (the azimuthal angle in the xy-plane). The nth power is then given by
vn=rn(sin⁡(nθ)cos⁡(nϕ)sin⁡(nθ)sin⁡(nϕ)cos⁡(nθ)),
v^n = r^n \\begin{pmatrix} \\sin(n \\theta) \\cos(n \\phi) \\\ \\sin(n \\theta) \\sin(n \\phi) \\\ \\cos(n \\theta) \\end{pmatrix},
vn=rn​sin(nθ)cos(nϕ)sin(nθ)sin(nϕ)cos(nθ)​​,
which scales the radius by $ r^n $ and multiplies the angles by $ n $, before converting back to Cartesian coordinates for the iteration.[\[4\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-4)[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3) The process begins at the origin $ v\_0 = (0, 0, 0) $, with $ c $ added after each power operation, ensuring the transformation preserves the rotational symmetry needed for fractal structure in three dimensions.[\[4\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-4)No canonical three-dimensional analog to the [Mandelbrot set](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbrot_set) exists, as $ \\mathbb{R}^3 $ lacks a normed [division algebra](https://grokipedia.com/page/Division_algebra) like the complex numbers for two dimensions or quaternions for four dimensions, leading to heuristic extensions such as the Mandelbulb's spherical formulation.[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3)

### History

The [Mandelbulb](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb) was developed collaboratively by amateur [fractal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal) enthusiasts Daniel White and Paul Nylander starting in November 2007 on the Fractal Forums online community. White published the initial [formula](https://grokipedia.com/page/Formula) for a degree-2 version (sometimes called the Mandelbug), while Nylander refined it by suggesting higher powers, such as 8, to reveal more intricate [fractal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal) details.[\[2\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-2)[\[1\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-1) The first three-dimensional rendering of the power-2 [Mandelbulb](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb) was created by Thomas Ludwig on November 20, 2007.[\[2\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-2) Earlier explorations of similar ideas date back to Rudy Rucker's experiments in 1988 and Jules Ruis's Basic program in 1997, but the 2007 formulation marked the modern discovery.[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3) The [Mandelbulb](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb) gained widespread attention in 2009 through deep zoom renders and media coverage, such as a [New Scientist](https://grokipedia.com/page/New_Scientist) article on November 18, 2009, highlighting its organic, self-similar structures.[\[1\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-1)[\[2\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-2)

## Mathematical Formulation

### General Framework

The Mandelbulb is a three-dimensional [fractal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal) set defined through an iterative mapping process in R3\\mathbb{R}^3R3, extending the concept of the two-dimensional [Mandelbrot set](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbrot_set) to higher dimensions while preserving self-similar properties. The process begins with the initial vector v0=(0,0,0)\\mathbf{v}\_0 = (0, 0, 0)v0​=(0,0,0) for a given parameter vector c∈R3\\mathbf{c} \\in \\mathbb{R}^3c∈R3, and iterates according to the map vn+1=vnp+c\\mathbf{v}\_{n+1} = \\mathbf{v}\_n^p + \\mathbf{c}vn+1​=vnp​+c, where p>1p > 1p>1 is a fixed power parameter that controls the degree of the transformation.[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3) This formulation assumes familiarity with basic fractal iteration, where sequences in the [complex plane](https://grokipedia.com/page/Complex_plane) are generalized to vector operations in three-dimensional [Euclidean space](https://grokipedia.com/page/Euclidean_space), treating c\\mathbf{c}c as the " [seed](https://grokipedia.com/page/Seed)" point analogous to complex parameters in the [Mandelbrot set](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbrot_set).[\[6\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-6)To compute the powering operation vp\\mathbf{v}^pvp meaningfully in 3D—beyond naive component-wise exponentiation, which lacks rotational invariance—spherical coordinates are employed, generalizing the polar coordinate approach used in the 2D Mandelbrot iteration zn+1=zn2+cz\_{n+1} = z\_n^2 + czn+1​=zn2​+c. A vector v=(x,y,z)\\mathbf{v} = (x, y, z)v=(x,y,z) is first decomposed into its spherical form: radius r=∥v∥=x2+y2+z2r = \\\|\\mathbf{v}\\\| = \\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}r=∥v∥=x2+y2+z2​, polar angle θ=arccos⁡(y/r)\\theta = \\arccos(y / r)θ=arccos(y/r), and azimuthal angle ϕ=\\atantwo(x,z)\\phi = \\atantwo(x, z)ϕ=\\atantwo(x,z). The powered vector is then obtained by scaling the radius to rpr^prp and multiplying the angles by ppp, yielding θ′=pθ\\theta' = p \\thetaθ′=pθ and ϕ′=pϕ\\phi' = p \\phiϕ′=pϕ, before converting back to Cartesian coordinates via:
x′=rpsin⁡(θ′)sin⁡(ϕ′),y′=rpcos⁡(θ′),z′=rpsin⁡(θ′)cos⁡(ϕ′).
\\begin{align\*}
x' &= r^p \\sin(\\theta') \\sin(\\phi'), \\\
y' &= r^p \\cos(\\theta'), \\\
z' &= r^p \\sin(\\theta') \\cos(\\phi').
\\end{align\*}
x′y′z′​=rpsin(θ′)sin(ϕ′),=rpcos(θ′),=rpsin(θ′)cos(ϕ′).​
This geometric interpretation ensures the transformation respects the spherical symmetry of 3D space, producing intricate, bulbous structures with recursive detail.[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3)[\[6\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-6)Membership in the Mandelbulb set is determined using an escape-time [algorithm](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Algorithm): for each c\\mathbf{c}c, the iteration proceeds until either ∥vn∥>R\\\|\\mathbf{v}\_n\\\| > R∥vn​∥>R (where RRR is a bailout [radius](https://grokipedia.com/page/Radius), commonly 2 or 4) or a maximum [iteration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Iteration) count NNN (e.g., 100–255) is reached without escape. Points c\\mathbf{c}c for which the sequence {vn}\\{\\mathbf{v}\_n\\}{vn​} remains bounded—i.e., does not diverge to infinity—are considered part of the set, mirroring the boundedness criterion of the [Mandelbrot set](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbrot_set).[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3) The choice of p=8p = 8p=8 serves as the baseline for the original formulation, balancing complexity and visual coherence, though the framework accommodates other integer powers.[\[6\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-6)

### Original Power-8 Formula

The original Mandelbulb formulation uses p=8p = 8p=8 in the general iterative [map](https://grokipedia.com/page/Map) vn+1=vn8+c\\mathbf{v}\_{n+1} = \\mathbf{v}\_n^8 + \\mathbf{c}vn+1​=vn8​+c. This power was selected by Daniel White and Paul Nylander after experimentation, as lower powers (e.g., 2) produce structures more akin to 2D fractals, while higher powers create increasingly bulbous and spherically symmetric forms; p=8p = 8p=8 achieves a desirable balance of intricate, self-similar details resembling organic shapes without excessive [computational complexity](https://grokipedia.com/page/Computational_complexity).[\[2\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-2)[\[4\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-4) The powering operation follows the spherical coordinate method described in the general framework, with the radius raised to the 8th power and angles multiplied by 8, ensuring rotational invariance and rich [fractal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal) structure.[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3)

### Iteration and Boundedness

The iteration process for the Mandelbulb, using the original power-8 formula, starts by initializing the vector v0=0\\mathbf{v}\_0 = \\mathbf{0}v0​=0. Subsequent iterations compute vn+1=vn8+c\\mathbf{v}\_{n+1} = \\mathbf{v}\_n^8 + \\mathbf{c}vn+1​=vn8​+c, where c\\mathbf{c}c is the point in 3D space being tested, and the eighth power is evaluated by converting vn\\mathbf{v}\_nvn​ to spherical coordinates, raising the [radius](https://grokipedia.com/page/Radius) to the eighth power, multiplying the angles by eight, and converting back to Cartesian coordinates. This loop runs for a maximum number of [iteration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Iteration) s, such as 100, or halts early if the magnitude ∣vn∣\|\\mathbf{v}\_n\|∣vn​∣ exceeds a [bailout](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bailout) [radius](https://grokipedia.com/page/Radius), typically set to 4.[\[7\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-7)[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3)The Mandelbulb set comprises all points c\\mathbf{c}c for which the sequence vn\\mathbf{v}\_nvn​ remains bounded, meaning ∣vn∣\|\\mathbf{v}\_n\|∣vn​∣ stays below the bailout radius indefinitely. In practice, boundedness is approximated by checking whether the sequence escapes within the allotted maximum iterations; if it does not, c\\mathbf{c}c is considered part of the set.[\[3\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-3)For visualizations, escape-time coloring assigns hues to points outside the set based on the iteration count at which ∣vn∣\|\\mathbf{v}\_n\|∣vn​∣ surpasses the bailout radius, with lower counts yielding one color range and higher counts another, enhancing the depiction of the fractal's boundary structure.[\[4\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-4)Rendering the Mandelbulb demands high [iteration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Iteration) counts, often exceeding 100 and reaching thousands for deep zooms, owing to the [exponential growth](https://grokipedia.com/page/Exponential_growth) in complexity from the 3D power transformation, which amplifies the need for precise [orbit](https://grokipedia.com/page/Orbit) tracking to resolve intricate surface details.[\[7\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-7)

## Formula Variations

### Cubic Formula

The cubic formula represents the power-3 variation of the Mandelbulb, often implemented using spherical coordinates for isotropic [symmetry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Symmetry) or a Cartesian [polynomial](https://grokipedia.com/page/Polynomial) for axisymmetric cases around the x-axis. ### Rendering Techniques

Rendering the Mandelbulb primarily relies on [ray marching](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ray_marching) algorithms augmented by distance estimation techniques, which leverage signed distance functions (SDFs) to approximate the distance from any point to the fractal's surface. In this approach, rays are cast from the viewpoint into the scene, advancing in steps proportional to the SDF value until the surface is intersected, enabling efficient traversal of the complex 3D geometry without exhaustive [voxel](https://grokipedia.com/page/Voxel) sampling. This method is particularly suited to the Mandelbulb's intricate, self-similar structure, allowing for volumetric rendering and surface shading based on iteration counts from the escape-time algorithm.[\[4\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-4)[\[10\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-10)Key software tools facilitate these computations, with Mandelbulb3D serving as a prominent [freeware](https://grokipedia.com/page/Freeware) application available since [2010](https://grokipedia.com/page/2010), offering user-friendly interfaces for formula customization, real-time previews, and high-quality exports across Windows, [Linux](https://grokipedia.com/page/Linux), and Mac platforms. Complementing this are Fragmentarium, an open-source IDE that utilizes GLSL shaders for GPU-accelerated exploration of distance-estimated fractals like the Mandelbulb, and [Shadertoy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shadertoy), a web-based platform hosting numerous real-time GPU shaders that implement [ray marching](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ray_marching) for interactive visualizations. These tools often integrate optimizations such as adaptive step sizes and bounding volumes to balance detail and performance.[\[11\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-11)[\[12\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-12)[\[13\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-13)The rendering process incurs significant computational demands due to the intensive 3D iterations required for each ray, often resulting in render times of minutes to hours per frame on standard hardware. To address this, optimizations include octree-based spatial partitioning to prune empty regions and early ray termination when opacity thresholds are met, alongside GPU parallelization via [CUDA](https://grokipedia.com/page/CUDA) or [OpenCL](https://grokipedia.com/page/OpenCL) for cluster-scale processing. For deep zooms revealing fine details, precision limitations in [floating-point arithmetic](https://grokipedia.com/page/Floating-point_arithmetic) necessitate higher-precision arithmetic or adaptive [iteration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Iteration) schemes, though [perturbation theory](https://grokipedia.com/page/Perturbation_theory)—typically used in 2D fractals to reduce redundant calculations—has limited direct application in 3D contexts but inspires similar delta-based approximations.[\[10\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-10)[\[14\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-14)[\[15\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-15)Common output formats encompass high-resolution still images for static analysis, animations generated through keyframe tweening and sequence rendering, and immersive VR experiences via 360-degree stereoscopic projections. Typical resolutions reach 4K (3840×2160) with supersampling anti-aliasing—employing 9 to 45 sub-samples per pixel—to smooth edges and minimize artifacts in the fractal's intricate surfaces.[\[16\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-16)[\[17\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-17)[\[18\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-18)

## Applications

### Uses in Media

The Mandelbulb has been employed in visual effects for several major films, leveraging its intricate, self-similar structures to depict otherworldly environments and entities. In the 2014 Disney animated film _Big Hero 6_, the climactic portal sequence features a [wormhole](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wormhole) interior rendered using a Mandelbulb [algorithm](https://grokipedia.com/page/Algorithm), with customized parameters to create swirling, [fractal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal)-like visuals that enhance the sci-fi action.[\[19\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-19) Similarly, the 2017 Marvel film _Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2_ incorporates 3D [fractal art](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal_art) generated with Mandelbulb3D software by artist Hal Tenny to form exotic planetary landscapes, marking an early high-profile integration of the fractal into Hollywood production design.[\[20\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-20)In the 2018 science fiction film _Annihilation_, directed by [Alex Garland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Alex_Garland), Mandelbulb-inspired fractals were used in the design of the surrounding crystalline structures and the Shimmer, including a translucent wall streaming with bulbous forms, as well as environmental elements like spores and [lichen](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lichen), achieved through [procedural modeling](https://grokipedia.com/page/Procedural_modeling) in [visual effects](https://grokipedia.com/page/Visual_effects) pipelines.[\[21\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-21)[\[22\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-22) These applications highlight the Mandelbulb's utility in creating surreal, biologically evocative imagery that blends mathematical precision with narrative immersion.Beyond feature films, the Mandelbulb appears in independent CGI shorts and [music videos](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dave_Meyers_videography), often produced using accessible tools like Mandelbulb3D to explore abstract, hypnotic animations. For instance, artist Julius Horsthuis has created animations such as "Our Fractal Brains" (2015), a [short film](https://grokipedia.com/page/Short_film) that navigates Mandelbulb geometries synchronized to [ambient music](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ambient_music), screened at festivals and online platforms.[\[23\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-23) Arthur Stammet's series of Mandelbulb3D-based shorts, including "Communication Craze in a Morphing World" (2012) and "Light Beings" (2025), combine [fractal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal) fly-throughs with cinematic storytelling and soundtracks, distributed primarily on [YouTube](https://grokipedia.com/page/YouTube).[\[24\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-24)The adoption of the Mandelbulb in media evolved rapidly after its 2009 discovery, transitioning from niche [fractal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fractal) enthusiast renders to mainstream [visual effects](https://grokipedia.com/page/Visual_effects) by the mid-2010s, facilitated by [open-source software](https://grokipedia.com/page/Open-source_software) that enabled efficient rendering of complex scenes for film and digital content.[\[20\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-20) This progression underscores rendering techniques like [ray marching](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ray_marching), which allow high-quality outputs suitable for integration into professional VFX workflows.[\[22\]](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mandelbulb#ref-22)
